How to choose a short-term rental market in 2026.

A decision framework for moving from a wide-open map to one market, one neighborhood and one property you can defend on paper.

In this guide1. Durable demand2. Rule stack3. Seasonality4. Neighborhood5. Taxes & insurance6. Underwriting7. Scorecard

1. Look for durable demand—not one hot year.

A short-term rental is a small hospitality business attached to a piece of real estate. The market has to give travelers a reason to arrive before the property can persuade them to book.

Begin with trip drivers. Parks, beaches and ski areas are obvious, but they are not the only durable sources of demand. Hospitals, universities, wedding venues, sports complexes, corporate offices, military installations, festivals and family visitation can fill different parts of the calendar.

The stronger market is often the one with several ordinary reasons to visit, not one spectacular reason.

Questions to ask

  • Who is the guest, and what causes the trip?
  • How many independent trip drivers exist within a reasonable drive?
  • Which months rely on a single event or weather pattern?
  • Does the market attract weekday stays, weekends, or both?
  • What would make a guest choose another nearby market?

2. Clear the complete rule stack.

“STR-friendly” is not a property-level conclusion. State law may allow short-term rentals while a city requires a license, a county limits eligible zoning, and an HOA prohibits the use entirely. Review every layer before you spend meaningful diligence money.

Regulatory due-diligence list

  • State statutes and lodging-tax registration
  • County zoning, land-use and fire-safety rules
  • City permit or license requirements
  • HOA, condominium and planned-community restrictions
  • Deed restrictions and title exceptions
  • Occupancy, parking, noise and local-contact rules
  • Renewal terms and transferability after a sale
  • Platform listing-number and tax-display rules

Save the official page, the date reviewed and the name of the official who confirmed the interpretation. Regulations can change between underwriting and closing.

3. Respect the calendar.

Annual occupancy can hide a weak shoulder season. Build a month-by-month view of nightly rate, occupancy, minimum-stay behavior and operating costs. Then ask whether the low months coincide with large fixed expenses or weather risk.

Seasonality is not automatically bad. A highly seasonal property can work when the purchase basis is right, peak pricing is strong and the owner holds adequate reserves. The mistake is underwriting the full year like the best twelve weeks.

4. Win at the micro-location.

Travelers do not book a metro area in the abstract. They book a promise: walk to dinner, reach the trail in ten minutes, park without stress, see the mountain from the hot tub, or get the whole family to the attraction quickly.

Drive the route at arrival time. Test the cellular signal. Look at grade, lighting, noise and winter access. Compare the best-performing listings inside the same guest decision set—not just within the same ZIP code.

Micro-location signals

  • True drive time to the primary attraction
  • Walkability that feels comfortable to a visitor
  • View corridors and the risk they may be blocked
  • Road quality, grade and weather access
  • Parking that matches permitted occupancy
  • Noise exposure and neighbor proximity
  • Proximity to cleaning, maintenance and emergency support

5. Price taxes, insurance and friction early.

Purchase price is only the front door. Confirm lodging and sales taxes, property-tax treatment, business registrations, utilities, trash, internet, snow or pool service, cleaning, maintenance, pest control and professional management.

Insurance deserves its own written quote. A platform guarantee is not a substitute for a policy designed for the actual use. Geography can introduce wind, wildfire, flood, freeze, roof or liability constraints that change the deal before revenue moves at all.

6. Underwrite an ordinary year.

Use a competitive set that resembles the property you intend to operate. Adjust for bedrooms, guest count, design quality, amenities, view, access and review history. Avoid treating the top listing as the baseline.

Model at least three cases: base, downside and disruption. The disruption case should include a meaningful revenue decline, a repair, a longer vacancy or a regulatory delay. If one bad quarter forces a sale, the property is not conservatively financed.

This guide is educational and cannot replace advice from local counsel, a CPA, an insurance professional or a property-level inspection.

7. Make the decision visible.

Score each market on durable demand, regulatory fit, economic resilience, seasonality and operational fit. Then document the evidence behind every score. The goal is not mathematical certainty; it is to expose where optimism is doing the work.

Before you tour a property

  • I can name the primary guest and at least three demand drivers.
  • I have verified the relevant rule stack with official sources.
  • I understand the market’s low season and operating risks.
  • I know which neighborhoods solve the guest’s trip best.
  • I have current tax and insurance assumptions.
  • I can explain why the base case is ordinary—not aspirational.
